cards.explanation: The answer is that he asks why Balaam didn't come sooner. Balak, king of Moab, goes out to meet Balaam at the border (Numbers 22:36). Then he opens with, “Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why did you not come to me?” (Numbers 22:37). No small talk at all. My mustache would've at least tried a hello.

The answer is that Balaam must speak only the word God gives him. Balaam, the man Balak sent for, doesn't blink. He says, “I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth.” (Numbers 22:38). The king had just talked about rewards, and Balaam answers with who he answers to. Friends, that's a short sentence with a lot of weight in it.

The answer is the outskirts of Israel's camp. The next morning Balak, king of Moab, brings Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, and “…he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.” (Numbers 22:41). That's what the text gives for the view. Think of spotting my bakery's front step from a hill.

The answer is False, and here's what the text says. Balaam asks for seven altars, seven bulls and seven rams (Numbers 23:1), and Balak, king of Moab, does as he's told (Numbers 23:2). The text records no pushback at all. I'd have wanted at least one question about that order, probably two.

The answer is that the LORD will meet with him. Balaam says, “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me.” (Numbers 23:3). He's hoping for a meeting with God, not a meeting with the wishes of Balak, king of Moab. And he adds that whatever the LORD reveals to him, he will tell the king.

The answer is message. The text says the LORD “…put a message in Balaam’s mouth…” (Numbers 23:5). Then Balaam is told, “Return to Balak and give him this message.” He carries what he was given. I know what it's like to deliver a cookie box exactly as packed.

The answer is God. Balaam asks, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8). His question rests on what God has done. The next line asks the same thing with the LORD's name: “How can I denounce those whom the LORD has not denounced?”

The answer is True. Balaam asks, “Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel?” (Numbers 23:10). That's a lot of people, friends. I once tried to count sprinkles, and I lost track somewhere around hello.

The answer is to die the death of the righteous. Balaam says, “Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (Numbers 23:10). He has just been looking at Israel, and that's the wish that comes out. I think that's a surprising thing for a man to say with the king of Moab standing right there.

The answer is that Balaam has only blessed them. Balak, king of Moab, says it plainly: “I brought you here to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them!” (Numbers 23:11). Notice the word only. He didn't get one curse mixed in, he got a blessing the whole way through. I think that's the longest face a king has ever made.

The answer is the top of Pisgah. The text says Balak, king of Moab, took Balaam “…to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah…” (Numbers 23:14). New spot, same plan. The king is hoping a different view will give him a different answer.

The answer is that Balak asks what the LORD said. When Balaam returns, Balak, king of Moab, asks, “What did the LORD say?” (Numbers 23:17). This time he's the one asking for the message. I think he already suspects what's coming.

The answer is that God does not lie or change His mind. Balaam says, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind.” (Numbers 23:19). He follows it with two questions: “Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?” Balak, king of Moab, had been hoping a new mountain might change the answer, and Balaam says it won't.

The answer is that Balaam cannot change it. He says, “I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it.” (Numbers 23:20). That follows right after he said God does not change His mind. Balaam isn't the one holding the dial.

The answer is Egypt. Balaam says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). So in the middle of this oracle he points back to where Israel came from. It's the strength of God that brought them out.

The answer is False, and here's what the text says: “For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel.” (Numbers 23:23). That means no spell works, not even a good one. Balak, king of Moab, is out of options on that front.

The answer is only after they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain. That's how Balaam's picture goes: “…not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). The people rise like a lioness and rouse themselves like a lion, and they don't rest until those things happen. It's a heavy image, and Balaam leaves it just as it is.

The answer is True. Balak, king of Moab, says, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (Numbers 23:25). Earlier he asked for a curse (Numbers 23:13), so this is a big change. I think two blessings in a row changed his order.

The answer is that God will allow a curse from there. Balak, king of Moab, says, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). He's hoping God might let a curse happen if the spot is different. I think the king is trying a new view for the third time and hoping for a different answer.

The answer is the top of Peor. The text says, “And Balak took Balaam to the top of Peor, which overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). That's spot number three for Balak, king of Moab. He's now running through mountaintops like a man checking every drawer for his keys.

The answer is the wasteland. The text says Peor “…overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). That's the third spot Balak, king of Moab, picks, and I think he's running low on scenic options. Wasteland is the word to keep.
